core: Working definition: minerals are inorganic elements the body needs in small amounts for structure and function (attributed to MedlinePlus: the body uses minerals for many jobs, including keeping bones, muscles, heart, and brain working properly)

Macrominerals vs trace minerals: macrominerals needed in larger amounts (calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, sodium, potassium, chloride, sulfur); trace minerals needed in tiny amounts (iron, manganese, copper, iodine, zinc, cobalt, fluoride, selenium)
The jobs: bones and teeth (calcium), nerve signals (calcium, sodium, potassium), fluid balance (sodium, potassium), oxygen transport (iron via hemoglobin)

One line each for calcium (most abundant mineral; stored in bones and teeth), iron (oxygen carrier in red blood cells), sodium (nerves, muscles, fluid balance), potassium (kidney and heart function, muscle contraction, nerve transmission)
Where they come from: minerals begin in soil and water, pass into plants, then into animals, and reach people through foods from both plants and animals
Getting them from food: most people get the amount of minerals they need by eating a wide variety of foods

Deficiency and excess both matter: too little iron draws down stored iron and can lead to anemia; too little calcium can weaken bones; too little potassium can raise blood pressure; excess sodium is common and can raise blood pressure
Honest framing: minerals are the body's hardware, vitamins its software; both are essential and need each other
supporting: Electrolytes (sodium, potassium) are a sibling topic; this lesson references them only for fluid balance
Kidney disease can require limiting potassium (MedlinePlus example of a health condition changing mineral needs); noted factually, no medical advice
Example daily amounts illustrating the macromineral/trace gap: calcium about 1,000 mg/day for adults, iron 8 mg/day for adult men and 18 mg/day for adult women
Original worked example tracing minerals through a day of meals (cereal, milk, banana, lentils, cheese, broccoli, salmon, spinach)
outOfScope: Electrolyte chemistry, balance, and hydration physiology (own topic: nutrition:foundations:electrolytes)
Vitamins and the organic compounds' jobs (own topic: nutrition:foundations:vitamins)
Supplements, dosing, regulation, and supplementation advice (own topic: nutrition:foundations:supplements)
Water and hydration mechanics (own topics: nutrition:foundations:water, nutrition:foundations:hydration)
Individual mineral fact sheets in clinical detail (e.g., DRI tables for all life stages)

claims.claim: Minerals are inorganic elements the body needs in small amounts for structure and function; MedlinePlus states the body uses minerals for many different jobs, including keeping the bones, muscles, heart, and brain working properly, and that they are important for making enzymes and hormones.

Minerals divide into macrominerals, needed in larger amounts (calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, sodium, potassium, chloride, sulfur), and trace minerals, needed in small amounts (iron, manganese, copper, iodine, zinc, cobalt, fluoride, selenium).

Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body; almost all of it is stored in bones and teeth, giving them structure and hardness, and the body needs it for muscles to move and for nerves to carry messages.
Iron is a mineral the body uses to make hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to all parts of the body.

Sodium helps with the function of nerves and muscles and helps keep the right balance of fluids in the body; most people in the United States get more sodium in their diets than they need, and too much can lead to high blood pressure.

Potassium is needed for proper kidney and heart function, muscle contraction, and nerve transmission; getting too little can increase blood pressure, deplete calcium in bones, and increase the risk of kidney stones.

Most people get the amount of minerals they need by eating a wide variety of foods; minerals are found naturally in many foods from both plants (lentils, spinach, kale, broccoli, bananas) and animals (milk, yogurt, cheese, meat, seafood, sardines with bones).

Deficiency and excess both matter: in the short term, getting too little iron does not cause obvious symptoms because the body uses its stored iron, and too much sodium in the diet can lead to high blood pressure.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether minerals matter more than vitamins, or vice versa
positions: Popular marketing often elevates one micronutrient category, especially vitamins, as the key to health
Authoritative sources treat both as essential micronutrients with different but necessary jobs; neither can substitute for the other
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the hardware/software framing explicitly as an analogy with stated limits: minerals build the structures and machines, vitamins help the machinery run, and both are essential. No superiority claim is made.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether most people need mineral supplements to meet their needs
positions: Supplement marketing suggests widespread mineral gaps that only pills can close
MedlinePlus: most people get the amount of minerals they need by eating a wide variety of foods; some health conditions (e.g., chronic kidney disease) change needs and call for medical guidance
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the food-first guidance factually, notes that health conditions can change needs without giving advice, and leaves supplements entirely to the supplements sibling topic.

sourceRecords.title: Minerals (Health Topics)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Primary source for the working definition (the body uses minerals for many jobs, including keeping bones, muscles, heart, and brain working properly; minerals are important for making enzymes and hormones), the macrominerals list (calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, sodium, potassium, chloride, sulfur) vs trace minerals list (iron, manganese, copper, iodine, zinc, cobalt, fluoride, selenium), the guidance that most people get the minerals they need by eating a wide variety of foods, and the chronic kidney disease / potassium example of conditions that change needs.

sourceRecords.title: Calcium Fact Sheet for Consumers
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: calcium is a mineral needed to build and maintain strong bones; calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body; almost all calcium is stored in bones and teeth giving structure and hardness; needed for muscles to move and nerves to carry messages; adult recommended amounts (1,000 mg/day ages 19-50); food sources including milk, yogurt, cheese, sardines with bones, kale, broccoli, bok choy.

sourceRecords.title: Iron Fact Sheet for Consumers
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: iron is a mineral the body needs for growth and development; the body uses iron to make hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to all parts of the body; adult recommended amounts (8 mg/day men 19+, 18 mg/day women 19-50); food sources (lean meat, seafood, poultry, iron-fortified cereals, white beans, lentils, spinach, kidney beans, peas, nuts, raisins); short-term low intake uses stored iron without obvious symptoms.

sourceRecords.title: Potassium Fact Sheet for Consumers
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: the body needs potassium for almost everything it does, including proper kidney and heart function, muscle contraction, and nerve transmission; getting too little potassium can increase blood pressure, deplete calcium in bones, and increase the risk of kidney stones; food sources (dried apricots, prunes, raisins, orange juice, bananas, acorn squash, potatoes, spinach, tomatoes, broccoli, lentils, kidney beans, soybeans, nuts, milk, yogurt, meats, poultry, fish).

sourceRecords.title: Sodium (Health Topics)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22. Supports: the body needs some sodium to work properly; it helps with the function of nerves and muscles and helps keep the right balance of fluids in the body; the kidneys control how much sodium is in the body; if there is too much and the kidneys cannot remove it, sodium builds up and can lead to high blood pressure; most people in the U.S. get more sodium than they need.
